original_extraction.evidence_text:
The worst-case scenario is war. Your country attacks and the other one retaliates (or vice versa). As
both countries get pulled into a major war, the people of both nations suffer. Think of any major
war and the huge costs involved in terms of life, money and wellbeing.

---

Another scenario, better than the first but still far from satisfactory, is a temporary truce. Both
countries agree to a cease-fire, but there is no reconciliation. Resentment seethes beneath the
surface, and there is the constant underlying threat that war will break out again. Think of India and
Pakistan, with the constant threat of nuclear war, and the intense hostility between Hindus and
Muslims.

---

The third possibility is genuine peace. You acknowledge your differences and allow them just to be.
This doesn’t get rid of the other country, nor does it mean that you necessarily like it or even want it
there. Nor does it mean that you approve of its politics or religion. But because you’re no longer at
war, you can now use your money and resources to build up the infrastructure of your own country,
instead of squandering them on the battlefield.

---

The first scenario, war, is like the struggle to get rid of unwanted thoughts and feelings. It’s a battle
that can never be won and it consumes a huge amount of time and energy.

---

The second scenario, a truce, is definitely better, but it’s still a long way from true acceptance. It’s
more like a grudging tolerance; there’s no sense of moving forward to a new future. Although there
is no active warfare, the hostility remains, and you are resigned to the ongoing tension. A grudging
tolerance of thoughts and feelings is better than an outright struggle, but it leaves you feeling stuck
and somewhat helpless. It’s a sense more of resignation than of acceptance, of entrapment rather
than freedom, of being stuck rather than moving forward.
generation_rules: Use metaphorical scenarios of war, truce, and peace to illustrate psychological processes.
Contrast struggle, grudging tolerance, and acceptance to highlight therapeutic progress.
pause_rules: Pause after each scenario to allow reflection on the differences between struggle, tolerance, and acceptance.
original_extraction.psychological_function: Facilitates moving from struggle or grudging tolerance of internal experiences to genuine acceptance, enabling forward movement and reduced psychological entrapment.
repetition_rules: Repeat the metaphorical scenarios to reinforce understanding of different psychological states.
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Promotes acceptance of unwanted thoughts and feelings to reduce struggle and increase psychological freedom.
voice_rules: Use clear, illustrative metaphors to explain complex psychological states.
Adopt a didactic and explanatory tone.
